This page is a suggested 12-week syllabus for an introductory course in item
response theory (IRT), for graduate students in education, psychology or the
health sciences. Each week lists what students should be able to do by the
end of it, what to read on this site, what to run in R, and which lab and
dataset to use. Take it as a starting point: Drop weeks, merge them, or swap
in your own readings. The [instructor toolkit](instructor-toolkit.html)
helps with that: It builds labs on your own datasets and lets you edit the
built-in labs and add your own exercises.

The online book [*Item Response Theory with mirt and
mirtverse*](../book/index.html) has one chapter for each week below, with the
ideas, two worked examples on different data, exercises with solutions and a
pointer to the matching lab. Assign the chapter as the week's reading.

Everything here runs on a laptop with mirt and mirtverse installed. No
internet connection is needed once the packages are installed, and none of
the examples take more than a few seconds to run.

## Before the first class

Ask students to install the packages and check that a lab opens:

```{r}
install.packages(c("mirt", "learnr"))
# install mirtverse as shown on the home page, then:
library(mirtverse)
list_labs()
```

Students who are new to R can do much of the course without writing code.
The [workbench](workbench.html) (`launch_workbench()`) runs a full analysis by
pointing and clicking and shows the R code for every step, and
[`mv_ask()`](mv-ask-guide.html) writes a script from a plain-language request.
Both make good bridges to writing code by hand later in the term.

## The 12 weeks at a glance

| Week | Topic | Lab | Main data |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Measurement, scoring and classical item analysis | Lab 1, first two sections | `certexam` |
| 2 | From classical test theory to IRT: The Rasch, 2PL and 3PL models | | `LSAT7` |
| 3 | Estimation and comparing models | | `LSAT7`, `SAT12` |
| 4 | Dimensionality and local independence | [Lab 1](teaching-labs.html) in class | `certexam` |
| 5 | Item fit, person fit and item quality | | `SAT12` |
| 6 | Information, precision and reliability | | `certexam` |
| 7 | Scoring people | [Lab 2](teaching-labs.html) in class | `certexam` |
| 8 | Polytomous items and open-ended responses | Lab 6, `run_lab("open-ended")` | `openended`, `Science` |
| 9 | Differential item functioning and fairness | Lab 3, `run_lab("fairness")` | `numeracy`, `certexam` |
| 10 | Linking and equating | Lab 4, `run_lab("linking")` | `linking`, `certexam` |
| 11 | Item banks, test assembly and adaptive testing | Lab 5, `run_lab("cat-design")` | `catbank`, `certexam` bank |
| 12 | Cut scores, reporting and communicating results | Final project | students' own data |

The [glossary](glossary.html) defines each term used below, and each week
links to its key terms there. The [cheat
sheet](../cheatsheet/mirtverse-cheatsheet.pdf) lists the main functions on
two printable pages; both work well as handouts from week 1.

## Week by week

### Week 1. Measurement, scoring and classical item analysis

**By the end of the week, students can** score multiple-choice responses
against a key, compute proportion correct and item-total correlations, and
read a distractor analysis.

* **Key terms:** [Classical test theory](glossary.html#classical-test-theory),
  [sum score](glossary.html#sum-score), [p-value](glossary.html#p-value),
  [item-total correlation](glossary.html#item-total-correlation).
* **Read:** [Getting started](mirtverse.html); "The story" and "Start a lab"
  in [Teaching labs](teaching-labs.html).
* **Run:** `key2binary()`, `itemstats()` (mirt), `profile_data()`.
* **Lab:** The first two sections of Lab 1 (`run_lab("model-choice")`),
  "Score the responses" and "Screen the items". Students meet a miskeyed
  item without being told it is there.
* **Data:** `certexam`, `certexam_key`.
* **Discuss:** What a number-correct score can and cannot tell us.

### Week 2. From classical test theory to IRT

**By the end of the week, students can** explain the Rasch, 2PL and 3PL
models, fit them with `mirt()`, and read an item characteristic curve.

* **Key terms:** [Item response theory](glossary.html#item-response-theory),
  [latent trait](glossary.html#latent-trait), [Rasch
  model](glossary.html#rasch-model), [2PL](glossary.html#two-pl),
  [3PL](glossary.html#three-pl), [item characteristic
  curve](glossary.html#item-characteristic-curve),
  [difficulty](glossary.html#difficulty),
  [discrimination](glossary.html#discrimination),
  [guessing](glossary.html#guessing).
* **Read:** Sections 1 to 4 of [Getting started](mirtverse.html).
* **Run:** `mirt()`, `coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE)`, `gg_trace()`,
  `item_table()`, `interpret()`.
* **Data:** `LSAT7` (expand it with `expand.table()`).
* **Activity:** Ask students to sketch trace lines for items they invent
  (an easy item, a hard item, a flat item) and then find the closest real
  item in the data.

### Week 3. Estimation and comparing models

**By the end of the week, students can** describe marginal maximum likelihood
in words, recognise a model that has not converged, and compare nested models
with likelihood-ratio tests and information criteria.

* **Key terms:** [Calibration](glossary.html#calibration), [marginal maximum
  likelihood](glossary.html#marginal-maximum-likelihood),
  [convergence](glossary.html#convergence), [likelihood-ratio
  test](glossary.html#likelihood-ratio-test), [information
  criteria](glossary.html#information-criteria), [M2](glossary.html#m2),
  [RMSEA](glossary.html#rmsea).
* **Read:** "Let mirtverse pick a model" in [Getting started](mirtverse.html).
* **Run:** `select_model()`, `anova()`, `M2()`, `glance_mirt()`,
  `tidy_mirt()`.
* **Data:** `LSAT7` and `SAT12` (scored with `key2binary()`).
* **Discuss:** Why AIC and BIC can disagree, and what sample size has to do
  with fitting a 3PL.

### Week 4. Dimensionality and local independence

**By the end of the week, students can** check whether one dimension is
enough, read standardized residuals and the Q3 statistic, and tell local
dependence from a second trait.

* **Key terms:** [Dimensionality](glossary.html#dimensionality), [local
  independence](glossary.html#local-independence), [local
  dependence](glossary.html#local-dependence), [Q3](glossary.html#q3).
* **Run:** A one- vs two-factor model with `anova()`, `summary()` for rotated
  loadings, `residuals(mod, type = "Q3")` and `gg_q3()`.
* **Lab:** All of Lab 1 (`run_lab("model-choice")`, about 75 minutes). It
  ends with a model choice the student has to justify in writing.
* **Data:** `certexam` (the passage pair Q21 and Q22).
* **Assignment:** Hand in the decision table and justification from the end
  of Lab 1.

### Week 5. Item fit, person fit and item quality

**By the end of the week, students can** read S-X² item fit, compare an
empirical and a model-implied curve, and flag aberrant response patterns.

* **Key terms:** [Item fit](glossary.html#item-fit),
  [S-X²](glossary.html#s-x2), [empirical item
  curve](glossary.html#empirical-item-curve), [person
  fit](glossary.html#person-fit), [Zh](glossary.html#zh).
* **Run:** `itemfit()` and `gg_itemfit()`, `gg_empirical()`, `personfit()`
  (mirt), `item_card()` and `item_cards()`.
* **Data:** `SAT12`.
* **Activity:** Students pick the three weakest items from the item cards and
  write one sentence each on what an item writer should change.

### Week 6. Information, precision and reliability

**By the end of the week, students can** read item and test information
curves, convert information to a standard error, and explain why reliability
depends on where on the scale you look.

* **Key terms:** [Item information](glossary.html#item-information), [test
  information](glossary.html#test-information), [standard error of
  measurement](glossary.html#standard-error-of-measurement), [marginal
  reliability](glossary.html#marginal-reliability),
  [targeting](glossary.html#targeting).
* **Run:** `gg_info()`, `testinfo()`, `marginal_rxx()` and `empirical_rxx()`
  (mirt).
* **Lab:** The "Precision at the pass mark" section of Lab 2 previews next
  week.
* **Data:** `certexam`.

### Week 7. Scoring people

**By the end of the week, students can** compare EAP, MAP, ML and WLE
scores, explain why ML fails for perfect scores, and read a Wright map.

* **Key terms:** [EAP](glossary.html#eap), [MAP](glossary.html#map),
  [ML](glossary.html#ml-scoring), [WLE](glossary.html#wle), [Wright
  map](glossary.html#wright-map), [classification
  accuracy](glossary.html#classification-accuracy).
* **Run:** `fscores()` (mirt), `gg_scores()`, `gg_wright()`,
  `augment_mirt()`.
* **Lab:** All of Lab 2 (`run_lab("decisions")`, about 75 minutes). Students
  choose a scoring method, estimate classification accuracy, look for DIF
  and write a memo to the board. Lab 2 fits its own model, so students who
  missed Lab 1 can still do it.
* **Data:** `certexam`.
* **Assignment:** The memo from the end of Lab 2.

### Week 8. Polytomous items and open-ended responses

**By the end of the week, students can** fit the partial credit, generalized
partial credit and graded response models, read category curves, and say
when categories should be collapsed.

* **Key terms:** [Polytomous item](glossary.html#polytomous-item), [graded
  response model](glossary.html#graded-response-model),
  [GPCM](glossary.html#gpcm), [category response
  curve](glossary.html#category-response-curve), [QWK](glossary.html#qwk).
* **Read:** [Assessment pipeline](assessment-pipeline.html), section "9.
  Scoring", for scoring open-ended responses with `score_open()`.
* **Run:** `select_model()` on polytomous data, `gg_trace()`, `gg_info()`.
* **Lab:** Lab 6 (`run_lab("open-ended")`, about 75 minutes): Rater
  agreement and quadratic weighted kappa, rater severity and consistency,
  resolving two reads, PCM versus GPCM versus GRM, collapsing categories
  with disordered steps, and checking an automated scoring engine, including
  for subgroups.
* **Data:** `openended` (six rater-scored science tasks) in Lab 6;
  `Science` (four Likert-type items) for extra practice.
* **Students coming from ltm, eRm or TAM:** `mirtify()` translates their old
  code ([Coming from other IRT packages](mirtify.html)).

### Week 9. Differential item functioning and fairness

**By the end of the week, students can** tell impact from DIF, run a DIF
analysis with anchor items, and explain uniform and non-uniform DIF.

* **Key terms:** [DIF](glossary.html#dif), [reference and focal
  groups](glossary.html#reference-focal-group), [uniform and non-uniform
  DIF](glossary.html#uniform-nonuniform-dif), [DIF effect
  size](glossary.html#dif-effect-size), [anchor
  items](glossary.html#anchor-items).
* **Run:** `dif()`, `gg_dif()`, `interpret()` on the result; `multipleGroup()`
  and `DIF()` (mirt) for the model behind it.
* **Lab:** The "Fairness across languages" section of Lab 2 for a short
  version; Lab 3 (`run_lab("fairness")`, about 75 minutes) for a full
  session, with Mantel-Haenszel, anchor purification and differential test
  functioning.
* **Data:** `numeracy` (English language learners and fluent students) in
  Lab 3; `certexam` (English and French candidates) in Lab 2.
* **Discuss:** What a content review panel should do with a flagged item.

### Week 10. Linking and equating

**By the end of the week, students can** explain why two forms need a common
scale, describe anchor-item and common-person designs, and link a new
calibration to an existing one.

* **Key terms:** [Linking](glossary.html#linking), [anchor
  items](glossary.html#anchor-items), [moment
  linking](glossary.html#moment-linking), [characteristic curve
  linking](glossary.html#characteristic-curve-linking), [parameter
  drift](glossary.html#parameter-drift).
* **Read:** [Assessment pipeline](assessment-pipeline.html), sections "3.
  Field-test design" and "6. The item bank".
* **Run:** `design_field_test()`, `link_to_bank()`; `multipleGroup()` with
  anchors and `fixedCalib()` (mirt).
* **Lab:** Lab 4 (`run_lab("linking")`, about 75 minutes): Separate and
  concurrent calibration, mean-sigma linking, anchor drift and IRT
  true-score equating of a pass mark.
* **Data:** `linking` (two forms with common items) in Lab 4; `certexam`,
  split into two field-test forms by `design_field_test()`, for the pipeline
  functions.

### Week 11. Item banks, test assembly and adaptive testing

**By the end of the week, students can** describe an item bank, assemble a
form to a target information curve, and explain how a computerized adaptive
test picks items and when it stops.

* **Key terms:** [Item bank](glossary.html#item-bank), [automated test
  assembly](glossary.html#automated-test-assembly), [computerized adaptive
  test](glossary.html#computerized-adaptive-test), [multistage
  test](glossary.html#multistage-test), [exposure](glossary.html#exposure).
* **Read:** [Assessment pipeline](assessment-pipeline.html), sections "6. The
  item bank" and "7. Forms, adaptive and multistage tests".
* **Run:** `mv_bank()`, `assemble_forms()`, `simulate_cat()`,
  `assemble_mst()`.
* **Lab:** Lab 5 (`run_lab("cat-design")`, about 75 minutes): Bank
  information, a CAT by hand, simulation, exposure control, content
  balancing and stopping rules.
* **Data:** `catbank` (a 180-item placement bank) in Lab 5; the `certexam`
  bank built in the pipeline article for the pipeline functions.

### Week 12. Cut scores, reporting and communicating results

**By the end of the week, students can** describe a Bookmark standard
setting, estimate classification accuracy at a cut score, and explain IRT
results to someone who does not use R.

* **Key terms:** [Cut score](glossary.html#cut-score), [standard
  setting](glossary.html#standard-setting), [response
  probability](glossary.html#response-probability), [classification
  accuracy](glossary.html#classification-accuracy), [classification
  consistency](glossary.html#classification-consistency).
* **Read:** [Assessment pipeline](assessment-pipeline.html), sections "8. Cut
  scores" and "11. The report"; [Sharing results with a
  dashboard](dashboards.html).
* **Run:** `item_map()`, `set_cuts()`, `mv_report()`, `mv_dashboard()`.
* **Final project:** See below.

## An optional module: AI in measurement {#ai-module}

Four more weeks take the course into AI. They follow week 12 in a 16-week
term, or replace weeks 10 and 11 in a course that wants AI more than
linking and adaptive testing. Each week pairs an AI method with the
psychometric check that goes with it, uses one chapter of the
[book](../book/index.html) as the reading and one lab in class. Everything
runs offline: The labs use simulated data, and language-model examples run
from recorded answers (`mv_llm_replay()`). The [AI Hub](ai-hub.html) is the
students' starting page.

| Week | Topic | Lab | Main data |
|---|---|---|---|
| 13 | Machine learning through an IRT lens; item text and difficulty | Lab 8, `run_lab("item-text")` | `itemtext` |
| 14 | Automatic item generation and item families | Lab 9, `run_lab("aig")` | `aigfield` |
| 15 | Automated scoring and large language models | Lab 7, `run_lab("auto-scoring")` | `essays` |
| 16 | Validity, fairness and governance of AI | Lab 10, `run_lab("ai-audit")` | `aiscored` |

### Week 13. Machine learning through an IRT lens; item text and difficulty

**By the end of the week, students can** translate machine learning terms
into measurement terms, explain why a prediction model is judged by
cross-validation, and predict item difficulty from item text with an LLTM
and a lasso.

* **Key terms:** [Machine learning](glossary.html#machine-learning),
  [feature](glossary.html#feature), [overfitting and
  cross-validation](glossary.html#cross-validation),
  [LLTM](glossary.html#lltm).
* **Read:** Book chapters [Machine learning through an IRT
  lens](../book/ml-lens.html) and [What item text tells
  us](../book/item-text.html); the [translation table](ai-translation.html).
* **Run:** `item_features()`, `predict_difficulty()`.
* **Lab:** Lab 8 (`run_lab("item-text")`, about 75 minutes).

### Week 14. Automatic item generation and item families

**By the end of the week, students can** write an item model with
constraints, generate isomorphs, and check after a field test whether the
items of each family are equally difficult.

* **Key terms:** [Automatic item generation](glossary.html#aig), [item
  model](glossary.html#item-model).
* **Read:** Book chapter [Generating items](../book/aig.html); the
  [assessment pipeline](assessment-pipeline.html#stage-1-2), section "1–2.
  Item writing and review".
* **Run:** `item_model()`, `generate_isomorphs()`, `calibrate_families()`.
* **Lab:** Lab 9 (`run_lab("aig")`, about 75 minutes).

### Week 15. Automated scoring and large language models

**By the end of the week, students can** train a scoring engine, judge it
against human raters with QWK, SMD and PRMSE overall and within groups, and
describe safe uses of a language model in an analysis.

* **Key terms:** [Automated scoring](glossary.html#automated-scoring),
  [QWK](glossary.html#qwk), [PRMSE](glossary.html#prmse), [large language
  model](glossary.html#llm), [hallucination](glossary.html#hallucination).
* **Read:** Book chapters [Automated scoring](../book/auto-scoring.html) and
  [Large language models as a colleague](../book/llms.html).
* **Run:** `train_scorer()`, `agreement_report()`, `score_open()`,
  `mv_ask()` with `mv_llm_replay()`.
* **Lab:** Lab 7 (`run_lab("auto-scoring")`, about 75 minutes).

### Week 16. Validity, fairness and governance of AI

**By the end of the week, students can** audit an AI component for
agreement, differential scoring and drift, separate DIF caused by an engine
from DIF in an item, and write the validity argument for using its scores.

* **Key terms:** [Differential scoring](glossary.html#differential-scoring),
  [validity argument](glossary.html#validity-argument).
* **Read:** Book chapter [Validity, fairness and governance of
  AI](../book/ai-validity.html); the [reading list](ai-reading.html#validity),
  section "Validity, fairness and governance".
* **Run:** `ai_audit()`, `validity_argument()`, `dif()`.
* **Lab:** Lab 10 (`run_lab("ai-audit")`, about 75 minutes).
* **Assessment:** The lab's memo to the technical advisory committee makes a
  good final task for the module.

### On your own data

The [instructor toolkit](instructor-toolkit.html) has three section types
that teach these topics on your own data: `"item-features"` (needs the
text of your items), `"aig"` (needs the family of each item) and
`"ai-scoring"` (needs machine and human scores). Give the extra data to
`new_lab()`:

```{r}
new_lab("our-engine", data = "data/responses.csv",
        scores = "data/engine_scores.csv",       # machine, human1, human2, group
        sections = c("intro", "models", "ai-scoring", "reflection", "wrap-up"))
```

### A one-day workshop

For practitioners who already know IRT, the module fits in one day. Ask
participants to install the packages before they come and to read the [AI
Hub](ai-hub.html) page. The [workshop kit](ai-workshop.html)
(`copy_workshop()`) has the slides and a facilitator's guide for this
schedule.

| Time | Session | Material |
|---|---|---|
| 9:00 to 9:45 | AI in measurement: What changes and what does not | [AI Hub](ai-hub.html); book chapter [Machine learning through an IRT lens](../book/ml-lens.html) |
| 9:45 to 11:00 | Automated scoring | Lab 7, `run_lab("auto-scoring")` |
| 11:15 to 12:30 | Item text and difficulty | Lab 8, `run_lab("item-text")` |
| 13:30 to 14:45 | Automatic item generation | Lab 9, `run_lab("aig")` |
| 15:00 to 16:15 | Auditing an AI-scored test | Lab 10, `run_lab("ai-audit")` |
| 16:15 to 17:00 | Governance, and what to do on Monday | Book chapter [Validity, fairness and governance of AI](../book/ai-validity.html), section on governance |

With less time, keep Labs 7 and 10: Together they cover an engine from its
training to its audit.

## Assessment ideas

| Weight | Task | When |
|---|---|---|
| 20% | Lab 1 decision table and model justification | Week 4 |
| 20% | Lab 2 memo to the board | Week 7 |
| 20% | Two short problem sets (one on fit and precision, one on DIF or linking) | Weeks 6 and 10 |
| 40% | Final project: A full analysis of a dataset of the student's choice, handed in as an `mv_report()` or a dashboard plus a two-page memo | Week 12 |

For the final project, students can follow the [assessment
pipeline](assessment-pipeline.html) from calibration to the report. Its flags
point out what to check before each next step, which works well as a
checklist for the write-up.

## Adapting the course

* **A shorter course (8 weeks):** Combine weeks 2 and 3, and weeks 5 and 6;
  drop week 10 and treat week 11 as a lecture without a lab.
* **An undergraduate course:** Spend two weeks on week 1, use the
  [workbench](workbench.html) instead of code until week 4, and end at
  week 9.
* **A second course:** Add multidimensional and bifactor models (`mirt()`
  with more factors, `bfactor()`), [response-time models](response-times.html)
  (`fit_rt()`, `sim_rt()`), and the remaining stages of the [assessment
  pipeline](assessment-pipeline.html), such as test security and bank
  monitoring.
* **AI in measurement:** Add the [four-week AI module](#ai-module), or run
  it as a one-day workshop.
